typology.notes: Four sentence patterns, one per level: he (indefinite classifying), ʻo (definite equational), aia (locative), e (imperative). Every pattern puts its marker word FIRST, so the frame is read left to right from the marker. Frame slots carry no labels — the pattern is taught by the room's tutorial and the English target, not by the boxes.

_review_note: NEEDS KUMU REVIEW before shipping. Specific calls to check: (1) 'He kumu ʻo Kaleo' vs 'He kumu ʻo ia' — the ʻo subject marker on a personal name is treated as part of the subject block, not its own slot; (2) 'ʻO Leilani ke kumu' — fronted-predicate equational, and whether 'ke kumu' reads as the subject to a speaker; (3) 'Aia ʻo Kaleo i ke kula' — i vs ma for a school, both are taught as location markers here but only i is used in a slot; (4) 'E inu ʻoe i ka wai' — an imperative that keeps ʻoe, glossed to English as 'Drink the water.' with the literal 'You drink the water.' shown alongside. Vocabulary used by this pack: kumu, haumāna, kula, wai, inu, hale, hoaaloha, hele, ʻoe, and the names Kaleo, Leilani, Kimo. Every content word here is also matched in vocab.room.haw (Nā Hoa, Ke Kula, Hōʻailona, Hoʻopunipuni), so the two tracks review each other.

puzzles.prompt: Build “Kaleo is a teacher.” in Hawaiian: push the word blocks into the frame.

feedback.solved: ✦ He kumu ʻo Kaleo — “Kaleo is a teacher.” Walk back to the portal ✦

on_enter.speaker: narrator
on_enter.text: A new shelf, in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi. The boxes are blank here.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: Hawaiian says WHAT something is before it says WHO. The English order is the one that gets rearranged, not this one.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: The he pattern:  he + [what it is] + [who].   He haumāna ʻo Leilani.  —  “Leilani is a student.”

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: The boxes no longer tell you what they want. Press T for the target — it says, in English, the sentence you are building.

hints.text: Predicate first: the block that says WHAT someone is goes in before the block that says WHO.
he marks “a / an”. It opens the sentence, so it belongs in the leftmost box.
he · kumu · ʻo Kaleo  —  “Kaleo is a teacher.” aia belongs to a different pattern; leave it on the floor.

goalSpec.description: Target: “Kaleo is a teacher.” Build that sentence in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi. Three of the four blocks on this floor belong in the frame.

puzzles.prompt: Build “Leilani is the teacher.” in Hawaiian: push the word blocks into the frame.

feedback.solved: ✦ ʻO Leilani ke kumu — “Leilani is the teacher.” Walk back to the portal ✦

on_enter.speaker: narrator
on_enter.text: Same room, different “is”. This one names somebody.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: Last room: he kumu — “a teacher”, one of many. This room: ke kumu — “THE teacher”, the particular one.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: When the sentence names a definite one, it opens with ʻo instead:  ʻo + [name] + [the one they are].   ʻO Kimo koʻu hoaaloha.  —  “Kimo is my friend.”

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: So he cannot open this one. It is on the floor to be left there.

hints.text: This sentence points at one particular teacher, not just any teacher — so it cannot start with he.
ʻo marks the one being named, and it opens the sentence.
ʻo · Leilani · ke kumu  —  “Leilani is the teacher.”

goalSpec.description: Target: “Leilani is the teacher.” Build that sentence in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi. One block on this floor means “a”, not “the” — it has no box here.

puzzles.prompt: Build “Kaleo is at the school.” in Hawaiian: push the word blocks into the frame.

feedback.solved: ✦ Aia ʻo Kaleo i ke kula — “Kaleo is at the school.” Walk back to the portal ✦

on_enter.speaker: narrator
on_enter.text: Four boxes this time. Somebody is somewhere.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: Saying WHERE something is gets its own opening word: aia. It does the work English does with “is at”.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: The aia pattern:  aia + [who or what] + i + [the place].   Aia ʻo Leilani i ka hale.  —  “Leilani is at the house.”

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: That little i is a whole box of its own. It carries the “at”, and the place cannot arrive without it.

hints.text: aia opens every “is at” sentence — it takes the leftmost box.
After aia comes the one being located, then the small word that means “at”, then the place itself.
aia · ʻo Kaleo · i · ke kula  —  “Kaleo is at the school.”

solution.sentence: Aia ʻo Kaleo i ke kula.

goalSpec.description: Target: “Kaleo is at the school.” Build that sentence in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi. Four boxes, five blocks — one of them belongs to another pattern.

puzzles.prompt: Build “Drink the water.” in Hawaiian: push the word blocks into the frame.

feedback.solved: ✦ E inu ʻoe i ka wai — “Drink the water.” Walk back to the portal ✦

on_enter.speaker: narrator
on_enter.text: The last shelf. This one is not a statement — it is an order.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: A command opens with e. It turns the action word that follows it into “do this”.

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: The e pattern:  e + [do what] + [who] + [to what].   E hele ʻoe i ke kula.  —  “Go to school.” (literally: “You go to school.”)

guided_tutorial.speaker: narrator
guided_tutorial.text: English throws the “you” away when it gives an order. Hawaiian keeps it — so ʻoe still needs a box.

hints.text: An order opens with e, and the action word follows it immediately.
ʻoe means “you” — it comes after the action, and the thing you act on comes last.
e · inu · ʻoe · i ka wai  —  “Drink the water.” he and aia open other patterns; both stay on the floor.

solution.sentence: E inu ʻoe i ka wai.

goalSpec.description: Target: “Drink the water.” Build that command in ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi — Hawaiian keeps the “you” that English drops.
